name: GDPR
description: EU General Data Protection Regulation overlay. Activated by personal data, health data, children's data, or biometric data declarations. Covers GDPR requirements including lawful basis, data subject rights, security of processing, breach notification, and data protection by design.

evidence_requirements: Data protection policies implemented demonstrating compliance with GDPR principles (Art. 24)
Data protection by design and by default integrated into processing operations (Art. 25)
Codes of conduct or certification schemes adopted where applicable (Art. 40, 42)
Data Protection Officer (DPO) appointed where required and contact details published (Art. 37, Art. 38)
Accountability principle demonstrated — controller responsible for and able to demonstrate GDPR compliance (Art. 5(2))
Supervisory authority cooperation procedures in place (Art. 31)
Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) conducted for high-risk processing (Art. 35)
Prior consultation with supervisory authority where DPIA indicates high residual risk (Art. 36)
DPIA reviewed when nature, scope, context, or purposes of processing change
Human oversight mechanisms configured for agent operations where automated decisions significantly affect data subjects (Art. 22(3))
Safeguards implemented for automated decision-making — data subjects can request human intervention, express point of view, and contest decisions (Art. 22(3))
Human-in-the-loop (HITL) or human-on-the-loop (HOTL) policy documented and enforced for high-risk automated processing operations (Art. 22, recital 71)
Override and halt mechanisms tested — designated reviewers can intervene in agent decisions before or after execution
Records of processing activities maintained — controller and processor records per Art. 30
Records include categories of data subjects, categories of personal data, purposes, and recipients (Art. 30(1))
Records available to supervisory authority on request (Art. 30(4))
Data Processing Agreements (DPA) in place with all processors (Art. 28(3))
Processor agreements specify subject-matter, duration, nature, purpose, and type of personal data (Art. 28(3))
Sub-processor authorization process with same data protection obligations (Art. 28(2), Art. 28(4))
Data minimization principle applied — only personal data adequate, relevant, and limited to what is necessary (Art. 5(1)(c))
Storage limitation principle applied — personal data not kept longer than necessary for its purpose (Art. 5(1)(e))
Data retention schedule documented and enforced
Processor inventory maintained — list of all processors and sub-processors with processing descriptions (Art. 28)
Due diligence performed on processor selection — processors provide sufficient guarantees (Art. 28(1))
Processor monitoring — ongoing verification of processor compliance
Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) conducted for agent operations likely to result in high risk to rights and freedoms of data subjects (Art. 35(1))
Agent risk profile documents nature, scope, context, and purposes of processing; necessity, proportionality, and risk assessment (Art. 35(7))
Risk classification for each agent — Low/Moderate/High/Critical — based on data classification, autonomous action scope, and processing impact
Prior consultation with supervisory authority completed where DPIA indicates high residual risk that cannot be mitigated (Art. 36)
Appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure appropriate level of security for personal data (Art. 32)
Access controls implemented — access to personal data restricted to authorised persons on need-to-know basis (Art. 5(1)(f))
Authentication and authorisation mechanisms protect personal data from unauthorised access
Lawful basis documented for each processing activity — one of six lawful bases under Art. 6 applied
Purpose limitation principle applied — personal data collected for specified, explicit, and legitimate purposes only (Art. 5(1)(b))
Special category data (Art. 9) and criminal conviction data (Art. 10) processed only under explicit grounds

threshold_adjustments.reason: GDPR Art. 6 lawfulness of processing — every processing operation must have a documented lawful basis; scope violations are Art. 5 violations

evidence_requirements: Data protection by design — appropriate technical measures integrated into processing at design stage (Art. 25(1))
Data protection by default — only personal data necessary for each specific purpose processed by default (Art. 25(2))
Accuracy principle — personal data is accurate and kept up to date (Art. 5(1)(d))
Pseudonymisation and encryption of personal data implemented where appropriate (Art. 32(1)(a))
Appropriate technical measures ensuring ongoing confidentiality, integrity, availability, and resilience (Art. 32(1)(b))
Cross-border transfer safeguards applied for personal data leaving the EEA (Arts. 44-49)

threshold_adjustments.reason: GDPR Art. 32 security of processing — controllers must implement appropriate measures to ensure security level appropriate to the risk, including encryption

evidence_requirements: Records of processing activities include data categories, purposes, recipients, and retention periods (Art. 30)
Processing records serve as audit trail — demonstrate compliance with GDPR principles (Art. 5(2))
Logs of automated processing activities available for supervisory authority (Art. 30(4))

threshold_adjustments.reason: GDPR Art. 30 records of processing and Art. 5(2) accountability — processing must be documented to demonstrate compliance

evidence_requirements: Physical security measures protect personal data from unauthorised physical access (Art. 32(1)(b))
Organisational measures ensure only authorised persons have access to processing areas
Hardware and media containing personal data secured against theft or unauthorised access
Endpoint security measures protect personal data on devices (Art. 32(1)(b))
Remote access to personal data secured with appropriate technical safeguards
Mobile device management for devices processing personal data
Appropriate technical measures ensuring integrity and confidentiality of personal data — inputs to systems processing personal data validated and sanitised (Art. 5(1)(f))
Protection of personal data against unauthorised or unlawful processing including injection attacks that could cause unauthorised disclosure or alteration (Art. 32(1)(b))
Input validation procedures applied at all ingress points where personal data is received, including API inputs, tool responses, and retrieved context
Audit logs capture detected injection attempts and blocked malicious inputs to personal data processing systems (Art. 5(2), Art. 30)
Personal data breach detection capability — ability to identify and confirm breaches affecting personal data (Art. 33)
Breach assessment process — determine whether breach likely results in risk to data subjects (Art. 33(1))
Breach register maintained — documentation of all personal data breaches regardless of notification obligation (Art. 33(5))
Ongoing monitoring of processing systems for security and compliance with GDPR obligations (Art. 32(1)(d))
Regular testing, assessing, and evaluating effectiveness of technical and organisational measures (Art. 32(1)(d))
DPO monitoring of GDPR compliance and advising on data protection obligations (Art. 39)
Anomalous processing detection — identify unusual access patterns, bulk downloads, or exfiltration indicators
Security monitoring appropriate to risk level of processing (Art. 32(2))
Vulnerability scanning and penetration testing as part of security assessment program
Process for regularly testing, assessing, and evaluating effectiveness of security measures (Art. 32(1)(d))
Vulnerability management — known vulnerabilities in systems processing personal data addressed promptly
Audit of compliance with GDPR processing requirements, including lawful basis verification
Personal data breach notification to supervisory authority without undue delay and within 72 hours of becoming aware (Art. 33(1))
Breach notification includes nature, categories and numbers of data subjects and records concerned, likely consequences, and measures taken (Art. 33(3))
Incident response plan covers personal data breach scenarios
Human escalation paths configured for agent actions that trigger data subject rights under Art. 22 — automated decisions with significant effect routed to human reviewer (Art. 22(3))
Escalation SLAs defined for GDPR-relevant agent incidents — human reviewer acknowledges and responds within defined timeframe
Data subjects notified of right to obtain human intervention, express point of view, and contest automated decisions (Art. 22(3))
Escalation logs maintained with reviewer identity, timestamp, decision rationale, and outcome — available to supervisory authority on request (Art. 5(2))
Data subject notification where breach likely results in high risk to rights and freedoms — notification without undue delay (Art. 34(1))
Data subject notification in clear and plain language describing nature, consequences, and measures taken (Art. 34(2))
Notification exemptions documented when applied — data encrypted, measures mitigate risk, disproportionate effort (Art. 34(3))
Ability to restore availability and access to personal data in timely manner in event of physical or technical incident (Art. 32(1)(c))
Business continuity and disaster recovery procedures cover personal data systems
Recovery procedures tested to validate personal data can be restored without loss or corruption
Post-incident review to update data protection impact assessments where needed
Lessons learned documented and controls updated to prevent recurrence
Recovery procedures updated based on incident findings

reporting_obligations.assessment_type: No mandatory external audit under GDPR. DPAs (Data Protection Authorities) may conduct investigations. Certification schemes under Art. 42 are voluntary.
reporting_obligations.reporting_entity: Lead Supervisory Authority (LSA) under one-stop-shop mechanism for cross-border processing, or local DPA for purely national processing. Data subjects notified directly when breach poses high risk.

notes: GDPR requires data protection by design and by default (Art. 25), security of processing (Art. 32), and records of processing activities (Art. 30). This overlay adds GDPR-specific evidence fields and threshold adjustments on top of the AKSI v0.6 common-control catalog; controls without overlay-specific adjustments inherit the base AKSI definitions.
